# Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands

First listed: 2026-06-24 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/glasshouse) - 2026-06-24

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Jonathan DeCourcey argues that medical rescheduling can transform Glass House by opening higher-priced markets, lowering taxes and enabling a US listing. Eisman explicitly adopts the speculative margin thesis in his recap. The NYSE listing and first European hemp sale occurred, while the guest's pre-fall broad-rescheduling deadline failed. Export permits and state rules remain material, European cultivation already exists, and the proposed Medicare market is overstated. Eisman also converts a production-cost target into a current figure and confuses illustrative gross margin with operating margin. The larger earnings opportunity remains conditional.

The successful listing and hemp export are distinct from unproven interstate medical-cannabis economics. Guest errors are recorded separately; Eisman is responsible only for his explicit claims and closing adoption. The investment thesis remains unresolved, while its legal, cost and margin premises contain identifiable errors.

**Right** | Jonathan DeCourcey | investment thesis | major

[Source at 2:52-4:14](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/glasshouse) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The company filing and regulatory changes document the constrained state-based structure; the cost mechanism follows from duplicated operations.

Qualification: Historical baseline before the new qualifying medical pathway.

Assessment test: Compare state licensing, production footprints and distribution rules.

- [Q2 2026 management discussion and analysis](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1848731/000184873126000031/glas-20260630xexx992.htm) (2026-08-14): The company deconsolidated dual-use retail June 12 to facilitate NYSE listing; NYSE trading began June 30. A first international hemp sale occurred in June. Cultivation remains based in California.
- [Initial statement of reasons for cannabis regulatory changes](https://cdn.cannabis.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/2026-04-r-20261030-isor.pdf) (2026-10-30): California describes pending regulatory work and the requirement for federal export permits to access international medical markets.

<a id="substack-203243827-c003"></a>
### 003. Schedule I classification means cannabis has no medical benefit and is highly addictive, but the medical premise is wrong.

**Mixed** | Jonathan DeCourcey | explanation | supporting

[Source at 2:52-3:37](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/glasshouse) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Scheduling refers to accepted medical use and abuse potential, not proof of no possible benefit or uniform addictiveness. HHS supports selected medical uses.

Assessment test: Separate statutory classification, clinical evidence and dependence risk.

- [Basis for recommending marijuana in Schedule III](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/scheduling-recommendation.pdf) (2023-08-29): HHS recommended Schedule III based on accepted medical use and lower abuse potential; it did not find cannabis incapable of causing dependence.
- [Drug scheduling](https://www.dea.gov/drug-information/drug-scheduling) (undated): Schedule III does not mean nonaddictive; it includes dependence potential and accepted medical uses.

### 045. The jump from $200 to $1,000 would be essentially all incremental margin because the same cannabis is being repriced.

### 046. With approximately $100 unit cost, gross margins could rise from 50% in California toward 88-90% or more in other markets.

Assessment test: Measure net selling prices and complete cost of goods sold.

### 063. Glass House could move from a 50% operating margin to an 80-90% operating margin because exports mostly add price rather than cost.

The illustrative unit arithmetic is gross margin, not operating margin. Q1 consolidated gross margin was only 25% with negative adjusted EBITDA; future operating margins are not established.

Assessment test: Subtract all operating expenses from a consistent gross-profit forecast.

## Framework and tools

- Compare a restricted local market with potential expanded-market economics.
- Separate current operations, installed capacity, targets and realized production.
- Treat legal reform, licensing and distribution implementation as distinct milestones.
- Use price-volume-cost scenarios while retaining incremental expenses.
- Separate a successful exchange listing from investment returns and operating success.
- Disclose ownership and distinguish speculative opportunity from modeled valuation.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Schedule I/III classification and Section 280E
- Banking and listing access
- Q1 revenue and loss
- Greenhouse footprint and annual biomass capacity
- Cost per pound and wholesale prices
- California versus US medical and European market pricing
- Gross-margin price sensitivity
- International import volumes
- Reverse stock split and exchange-listing conditions

## Source cautions

SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Jonathan DeCourcey, identified as Glass House head of investor relations. Very short interjections are occasionally embedded within the other speaker's segment; attribution follows the surrounding question and response.
- The publication is June 24, but the guest refers to May 26 as current and April changes as roughly a month earlier. Treat late-May recording as an inference, not a verified exact date.
- DeCorsi is normalized to Jonathan DeCourcey from the identified company role.
- The guest repeatedly says April 18; the inspected medical rule was issued April 23 and published April 28.
- The 1920-second can/cannot institutional-ownership interjection is ambiguous and is not silently corrected.
- The guest initially says target selling price then explicitly corrects to target production cost.
- Eisman's closing operating-margin language differs from the guest's gross-margin calculation.
- Publication follows June retail deconsolidation; original interview figures describe the earlier business perimeter.
- The first completed European transaction was hemp; it is not evidence of unrestricted marijuana exports.
